title: Erdős Problem #8: Monochromatic Covering Systems
description: For any finite coloring of integers, must there exist a covering system with monochromatic moduli? DISPROVED by Hough (2015) using the minimum modulus bound.

meta.author: Hough (2015)
originalContributions: CoveringSystem structure with covering property formalized
Coloring type and IsMonochromatic predicate defined
erdos_8_false theorem derived from resolution axiom

overview.historicalContext:
This problem was posed by Erdős and Graham in their 1980 book on combinatorial number theory. They conjectured that any finite coloring of the integers must admit a covering system whose moduli are all the same color.

The conjecture remained open until 2015, when Bob Hough's breakthrough on the minimum modulus problem for covering systems provided the key insight. Hough showed that the minimum modulus is bounded by 616,000, which creates a structural bottleneck exploitable to construct counterexamples.
overview.problemStatement:
**Coloring Version**: For any finite coloring of the positive integers, does there exist a covering system all of whose moduli are monochromatic?

**Density Version**: If $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $\sum_{a \in A, a > N} \frac{1}{a} \gg \log N$, must $A$ contain the moduli of some covering system?

**Answer**: NO to both. Hough (2015) disproved both versions.
overview.text: For any finite coloring of integers, must there exist a covering system with monochromatic moduli? DISPROVED by Hough (2015) using the minimum modulus bound.
overview.proofStrategy:
The key insight is Hough's **minimum modulus bound**: every covering system with distinct moduli has minimum modulus at most 616,000.

This creates a bottleneck:
1. Any covering system must include a "small" modulus (≤ 616,000)
2. Color all integers < 10^18 with distinct colors
3. Any covering system's moduli cannot all share a color
4. The sparse structure at the low end prevents monochromatic moduli sets

The formalization axiomatizes the minimum modulus bound and the resolution, then derives the falsity of the original conjecture.
keyInsights: Disproved using Hough's minimum modulus bound (2015)
Color small integers distinctly, large integers uniformly
Covering systems must 'start small' - creates bottleneck
Same technique disproves both coloring and density versions
Connects covering systems to Ramsey-type coloring problems

sections.title: Covering System Definitions
sections.summary: Defines CongruenceClass (residue mod modulus ≥ 2), CoveringSystem (a list of classes covering ℤ, with nonempty/covers fields), and the derived moduli finset and hasDistinctModuli predicate.
sections.mathContext: A covering system is a finite set of congruence classes $a_i \pmod{m_i}$ whose union is all of $\mathbb{Z}$; classically the moduli are distinct.

sections.title: Colorings
sections.summary: Defines the Coloring type (a function ℕ → Fin k), IsMonochromatic, and hasMonochromaticModuli — when all moduli of a covering system receive the same color.
sections.mathContext: A $k$-coloring assigns one of $k$ colors to each modulus; the conjecture concerns whether a monochromatic covering system always exists.

sections.title: The Original Conjecture (DISPROVED)
sections.summary: States the Erdős-Graham conjecture (erdos_graham_conjecture: every finite coloring admits a distinct-moduli covering system with monochromatic moduli) and its negation erdos_8_disproved.
sections.mathContext: Conjectured TRUE by Erdős-Graham; shown FALSE by Hough (2015). The distinct-moduli hypothesis is essential (else {0,1 mod 2} is trivially monochromatic).

sections.title: Hough's Minimum Modulus Theorem
sections.summary: Defines CoveringSystem.minModulus, states the axiom hough_minimum_modulus (every distinct-moduli covering system has minimum modulus ≤ 616,000), and derives balister_improved_bound from it.
sections.mathContext: Hough (2015): $\min_i m_i \leq 616000$ for any covering system with distinct moduli — the key structural obstruction.

sections.title: The Counterexample Construction
sections.summary: Describes Hough's coloring (each n < 10^18 gets a unique color, the rest share one) via hough_counterexample_coloring_exists, and proves erdos_8_resolution and erdos_8_false from bottleneck_counterexample + hough_minimum_modulus.
sections.mathContext: Coloring small numbers distinctly forces any covering system's mandatory small modulus to clash with another modulus's color, breaking monochromaticity.

sections.title: Density Version
sections.summary: Defines harmonicSumTail, HasLogDensityTail, and ContainsCoveringModuli, then states the disproved density_conjecture and the axiom density_conjecture_false: logarithmic tail density does not force containing covering moduli.
sections.mathContext: Even sets with $\sum_{a>N} 1/a \geq c\log N$ need not contain the moduli of a covering system — also disproved by Hough (2015).

sections.title: Why the Counterexample Works
sections.summary: Explains the bottleneck and proves the supporting theorems: single_class_not_covering (a modulus ≥ 2 misses an integer), covering_distinct_has_ge_two_classes, covering_distinct_moduli_card_ge_two, minModulus_mem, and the central bottleneck_counterexample (a pigeonhole coloring with no monochromatic covering — formerly an axiom, now PROVED).
sections.mathContext: Color each $n \leq 616000$ uniquely and all larger $n$ with color 0; the mandatory small modulus $m_1 \leq 616000$ then differs in color from any second distinct modulus.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Inventory and the combined theorem erdos_8_summary (both the coloring and density versions are false). Documents the 2 remaining axioms (hough_minimum_modulus, density_conjecture_false, reduced from 5) and the 9 proved theorems, including erdos_8_resolution and bottleneck_counterexample which were previously axioms.
sections.mathContext: Problem 8 is DISPROVED (Hough 2015): no finite coloring is forced to admit a monochromatic distinct-moduli covering system.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #8 is DISPROVED. Hough (2015) showed that not every finite coloring of integers admits a covering system with monochromatic moduli. The key is the minimum modulus bound: by coloring small integers distinctly, we can avoid monochromatic covering moduli.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: **Mathematical Impact:**

1. **Structural Rigidity**: Covering systems have inherent low-end structure that constrains their moduli sets

**2. Ramsey Connection**: Links covering systems to combinatorial coloring theory - some Ramsey-type properties fail

3. **Multiple Resolutions**: Hough's paper simultaneously resolved Problems #2 and #8 using the same techniques

4. **Density Insufficient**: Logarithmic tail density alone doesn't guarantee covering moduli.
openQuestions: What is the optimal minimum modulus bound?
Which specific colorings maximize the difficulty of finding monochromatic coverings?
Are there natural density conditions that DO imply covering moduli existence?
How does the minimum modulus bound affect other covering system properties?
